title: India Calls Out Pakistan's 'Genocidal Record' at the UN Security Council — and Kabul's Dead Are the Evidence
excerpt: At the annual UNSC debate on protecting civilians, Ambassador Parvathaneni turned Pakistan's Kashmir gambit into a catalogue of Islamabad's own atrocities — from the 1971 Operation Searchlight rapes to the 269 killed in the Kabul hospital airstrike.
body:
India's Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Harish Parvathaneni, delivered one of the sharpest diplomatic counterattacks in recent memory at the UN Security Council on Wednesday, dismantling Pakistan's attempt to raise Jammu and Kashmir at the annual open debate on the protection of civilians in armed conflict.

What was supposed to be Pakistan's familiar script — internationalize Kashmir, paint India as an occupier — instead became a forensic catalogue of Islamabad's own record of violence against civilians, stretching from the killing fields of 1971 Bangladesh to the bombed-out hospital corridors of Kabul in 2025.

The Kabul Hospital Strike That Changed the Calculus

Parvathaneni's most devastating salvo centred on Pakistan's airstrikes against Afghanistan earlier this year. During the holy month of Ramadan, Pakistani forces struck the Omid Addiction Treatment Hospital in Kabul — a facility that, by any definition under international humanitarian law, was a protected civilian object. According to the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan, the attack killed 269 civilians and injured 122 more. The strikes landed at the conclusion of tarawih evening prayers, when patients were leaving the facility's mosque.

The ambassador did not mince words. "The world has not forgotten that it was during a time of peace, reflection, and mercy that Pakistan conducted a barbaric airstrike on a facility which can by no means be justified as a military target," he said. More than 94,000 people were assessed as displaced by the cross-border armed violence, according to UNAMA.

Operation Searchlight and the 1971 Precedent

Parvathaneni then reached deeper into history, invoking Operation Searchlight — the codename for the Pakistani Army's campaign against the Bangladeshi nationalist movement in East Pakistan in March 1971. He cited the systematic campaign of mass sexual violence against an estimated 400,000 women, describing it as a "sanctioned" act of genocidal rape carried out by Pakistan's own military against its own citizens.

"Such inhuman conduct reflects Pakistan's repeated attempts over decades to externalise internal failures through increasingly desperate acts of violence both within and beyond its borders," the ambassador said. "With no faith, no law, and no morality, the world can see through Pakistan's propaganda."

Why This Matters at the UNSC

The annual open debate on civilian protection is one of the Security Council's most closely watched sessions. It draws statements from dozens of member states and carries symbolic weight, even if it rarely produces binding action. Pakistan has historically used this forum to inject the Kashmir narrative, knowing that the Council chamber lends it a veneer of international legitimacy.

India's response on Wednesday was notable not just for its bluntness — New Delhi has been sharpening its rhetoric at multilateral forums since the Pahalgam attack earlier this year — but for its strategic pivot. Rather than spending time defending its position on Kashmir, Parvathaneni chose to put Pakistan's civilian protection record on trial. The Kabul hospital strike, still fresh in the global consciousness, gave him evidence that no delegation in the chamber could easily dismiss.

The Diaspora Dimension

For India's global diaspora, the UNSC floor is where the country's diplomatic posture is most visibly tested. Indian-Americans, British Indians, and NRIs across the Gulf have long watched these exchanges with a mix of frustration and pride — frustration at Pakistan's ritual invocation of Kashmir, pride when India's response carries weight.

This exchange will likely resonate in diaspora communities that have been tracking a broader shift in India's foreign policy: from reactive defensiveness to proactive confrontation. The Pahalgam aftermath, the BRICS summit condemnation of terrorism, and now the UNSC riposte form a pattern that suggests New Delhi is no longer content to let Pakistan control the narrative at international forums.

What Comes Next

Pakistan's delegation is expected to exercise its right of reply, and the back-and-forth may continue in written statements. But the diplomatic damage may already be done. By linking Pakistan's Kashmir posturing to the Kabul hospital strike — an atrocity documented by the UN's own mission — India has created a rhetorical framework that will be difficult for Islamabad to escape in future debates.

The broader question for the Security Council is whether the protection-of-civilians agenda will remain a vehicle for bilateral score-settling, or whether member states will push for more substantive accountability mechanisms. For now, the debate has served as a reminder that the Council chamber, for all its procedural formality, remains one of the world's most consequential stages for geopolitical theatre.
